gabarito.reason:
This report is a false positive caused by where the key comes from. CryptoManager.encrypt calls Cipher.init(ENCRYPT_MODE, getKey()). getKey() first looks up the alias "secret" in the AndroidKeyStore. If the alias is missing, createKey() makes the key with KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES") and a KeyGenParameterSpec (purpose encrypt/decrypt, CBC, PKCS7, randomized encryption required). That generator is the only way the key ever comes into existence, and the key material never leaves the hardware-backed keystore. RVSec only saw the generator missing because the key was already in the keystore from an earlier run, or from an earlier write in the same session. In that case it was loaded through KeyStore.getEntry, a path the checker does not track. The key is not hard-coded, not derived from a password, and not built from bytes with SecretKeySpec. The IV is generated by the provider (randomized encryption is required) and stored with the ciphertext. Nothing in the code matches what the rule is meant to catch, so there is no real defect for a PR to fix and nothing worth an issue. A PR that 'fixes' this, for example by generating a fresh key on every encrypt or wrapping key creation so the checker sees it, would add risk without any security gain. Other concerns, such as CBC having no authentication, have nothing to do with this rule and do not justify sending something for this report.

Second judge: The runtime message alone does not prove insecure key generation: getKey() deliberately retrieves an existing AndroidKeyStore entry named "secret", whose generation may predate observation. However, createKey() has a concrete provider mismatch: KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES") does not select AndroidKeyStore, yet it is initialized with Android-specific KeyGenParameterSpec. Ordinary AES providers reject that specification, so first use without an existing key can fail instead of creating a persistent keystore key. A focused provider fix or an issue explaining this defect is justified. CryptoManager encrypts the local user-settings.json DataStore through UserSettingsSerializer; exported .keypass backups use the separate EncryptionHelper.
must_change: Explicitly select the AndroidKeyStore provider for AES key generation, for example KeyGenerator.getInstance(ALGORITHM, "AndroidKeyStore"), so the KeyGenParameterSpec creates the persistent "secret" entry used by getKey().
must_not_break: Decrypting the existing encrypted UserSettings DataStore file, which UserSettingsSerializer reads and writes through CryptoManager. Its on-disk format is [1-byte IV length][IV][AES/CBC/PKCS7 ciphertext]

Reusing the existing AndroidKeyStore key under alias "secret". Regenerating or replacing it on every call, or changing its alias, algorithm, block mode or padding, would make the stored settings unreadable
Keeping the key non-exportable inside AndroidKeyStore, rather than switching to app-held raw key bytes or SecretKeySpec
The provider-generated random IV (setRandomizedEncryptionRequired(true)), and the decrypt path, which relies on the stored IV
Loading settings at app startup on every supported Android version (the CryptoManager path is in the startup baseline profile)
Reuse the existing "secret" SecretKeyEntry. Do not regenerate or replace the key on every encryption or launch merely to make its generation observable.

Keep existing user-settings.json files readable: their format is one byte containing the IV length, followed by the IV and AES/CBC/PKCS7 ciphertext. Changing the alias or encryption format requires a migration that retains access to the old key and data.

Preserve all serialized settings, especially dbPassword, keyPassPassword and backupKey. Resetting settings on decryption failure can lose access to the SQLCipher database and disrupt authentication and backups.

Retain randomized encryption with a fresh provider-generated IV and encryption/decryption authorization. Preserve operation without per-use user authentication, including background automatic backups.
Support Android API 23 and later, including key creation on first use and retrieval and decryption after process restart.
Preserve the separate EncryptionHelper backup export/import format and existing .keypass backups; this provider fix requires no change to that format.

cards.notes: This is the expected one-line provider fix. The description correctly explains why it matters on Android 6 (minSdk 23). Runs that load an existing key still go through getEntry, so the checker would see the same thing.

Swapping getEntry for getKey reads the same keystore entry, so nothing about where the key comes from changes. At best it changes what the checker sees. The text honestly says the change was made only because RVSec flagged it.
It reaches the right conclusion (no security impact) but uses templated wording. It also calls the violation 'confirmed' instead of explaining why the key reuse is legitimate.
The provider fix is correct and minimal. The description accurately says the generator will now accept the keystore-specific parameters.
The issue raises CBC's lack of authentication, which has nothing to do with this report. What it says is accurate, but it doesn't justify sending anything for this finding.
It correctly and specifically explains the false positive: the key is loaded from the keystore on runs after the first. It also rightly sets aside the CBC concern.
Brief, but it correctly ties the finding to reuse of the keystore alias.
The issue is off-topic (CBC authentication). Its reason, 'could not establish the origin of the existing key', is wrong because the code shows createKey is the only source of the key.
The CBC authentication issue is unrelated to this report. It does correctly say that replacing the key would make saved settings unreadable.

It frames the outcome as 'violation real, no safe change could be made', which describes a failed attempt at a fix rather than a judgement that the code is fine. It also includes internal citations such as [C4].

The provider fix is correct, and the shared constant is a tidy touch. The description implies keys were previously stored somewhere else rather than explaining that the default AES provider rejects the parameters on API 23.
Like K93d1f1ab, it says the violation is real but no safe change was possible. That reflects a failed fix attempt and doesn't recognise the false positive.
The provider fix is correct. The description gives a misleading reason: keys created on another provider. The real problem is that key initialisation fails on API 23.
It correctly explains that the key is retrieved from the keystore under the alias, and that regenerating it would break existing settings.
A thorough and accurate analysis of where the key comes from, the IV handling, and why any change would only hide the call from the checker.
The overall conclusion is right. But it claims KeyGenerator falls back to another provider when initialisation fails, and that isn't true on API 23, which the app supports.

cards.regression_scenario: After this version rewrites user-settings.json with the version-2 byte and the secret_v2 key, downgrading to an earlier app build reads byte 2 as the IV length, decryption fails, and dbPassword and the other settings are lost. Later runs also still load secret_v2 through getEntry, so the finding remains.
cards.notes: It churns the key and adds a format change only to satisfy the checker, and still doesn't add the AndroidKeyStore provider. The description implies the report is resolved and falsely says the author ran the app under RVSec.
The provider fix is correct. The description accurately explains the Android 6.0 failure and that the alias and stored format are unchanged.
An accurate, code-specific explanation of the false positive.
It correctly identifies the keystore reuse that causes the false positive, and also checks that the IV handling is sound.
